before: A Ruby method that displays values with line endings.
after: Show a value on its own line.

before: A local name that can be assigned a value and later used to retrieve it.
after: A name that refers to a value within the part of the program where the name is available.

before: Ruby code that computes a number from numeric values.
after: A piece of Ruby code that works out a number.

before: A Ruby choice that runs a branch based on a condition.
after: Choose which path to take by checking a condition.

before: A Ruby loop that repeats its body while the checked condition is true.
after: Repeat a block while its condition counts as true.

before: A named group of Ruby instructions that can accept arguments and return a value.
after: A named piece of behavior you can call on an object, with inputs when needed.

before: The runtime that executes Ruby source and provides Ruby language behavior.
after: The program that reads Ruby instructions and runs them.

before: A Ruby value that has a class and can respond to methods.
after: A value that belongs to a class and can respond to method calls.

before: Division whose integer result follows the language’s integer rounding rule.
after: Divide two integers and round the answer down to a whole number.

before: The condition rule under which only false and nil are false-like.
after: Only false and nil count as false in Ruby conditions. Even zero counts as true.

before: Inserting an expression’s value into supported string syntax.
after: Insert the value of an expression into text using a hash sign and braces inside double quotes.

before: Two or more references reaching the same object rather than independent copies.
after: Two names refer to one object. Changes to that object can be seen through both names.

before: An immutable named Ruby value often used for identifiers or keys, distinct from a String.
after: A named value such as :topic. A symbol and a string with the same letters are different keys.

before: Reading an entry with a deliberate missing-entry policy rather than silently assuming presence.
after: Ask a collection for an item at a position or key. Fetch can use a supplied fallback if the item is missing.

before: A value or computation used for a missing key, which need not insert an entry.
after: The answer a hash gives for a missing key. Reading a simple default does not add an entry.

before: A range whose final endpoint is excluded from the represented interval.
after: A three-dot range leaves out its end value.

before: Explicitly skipping an iteration or leaving a loop rather than merely changing an output.
after: Next skips the rest of one turn. Break leaves the loop.

before: Selecting a when branch using each pattern’s matching behavior rather than assuming universal equality.
after: A case chooses the first when branch that matches the tested value.

before: The local names belonging to a method body rather than automatically sharing an outer local scope.
after: A method's parameters and local names belong to that call. Assigning a new value to a parameter need not change the caller's variable.

before: A method argument associated with a declared keyword name.
after: An input identified by a name such as topic:.

before: Ruby syntax for gathering or expanding keyword arguments, distinct from positional splat handling.
after: Two stars gather named inputs into a hash in a parameter list, or pass a hash as named inputs at a call.

before: Invoking the block supplied to the current Ruby method, with optional yielded arguments.
after: Run the block supplied to a method, passing it the given values.

before: A name explicitly limited to a block, which can shadow an outer local of the same name.
after: A name that belongs only to the block, such as a name declared after the semicolon in its input list.

before: The argument-count contract enforced by a Ruby lambda.
after: The number of inputs a lambda accepts. A call with the wrong count can raise ArgumentError.

before: A surrounding variable binding retained by a closure rather than an automatically frozen snapshot of its earlier value.
after: A closure keeps access to a nearby variable, so it can read a later value from that variable.

before: Calling a method unless its receiver is nil, without suppressing errors on other receivers.
after: The safe call sign skips a method when its receiver is nil.

before: An @name stores state on the current object.
after: A name starting with @ that stores a value on a particular object.

before: attr_reader creates methods that expose instance variables without generating writers.
after: A method that reads a stored property without automatically giving you a writer.

before: Public, protected and private determine ordinary method-call accessibility.
after: The rules for who can call a method. A public method and a private helper have different access.

before: A method associated with a particular object rather than all instances of its class.
after: A method defined on one particular object rather than every instance of its class.

before: super invokes the next method implementation in the lookup chain.
after: Ask the next implementation of the current method for its answer.

before: A module whose methods participate in another receiver’s method lookup.
after: A module that supplies methods another class can reuse.

before: A mixin operation that puts module methods before the class in lookup.
after: Put a module ahead of the class when Ruby searches for an instance method.

before: Unqualified constant lookup depends partly on the nesting of source definitions.
after: Ruby uses the scopes around a written definition when looking for a constant name.

before: Using an object through the behavior it supports rather than a required declared class.
after: Use an object for a behavior it supports without needing a particular class name.

before: Hash identifies keys using consistent hash values and eql?, not merely ==.
after: A hash uses its key comparison rules. Two numbers that compare equal with == need not be the same hash key.

before: Freezing an object does not automatically freeze the objects it references.
after: Prevent changes to the outer object. Objects held inside it can still be changeable.

before: Data defines immutable member bindings without enforcing deep immutability of members.
after: A Data object has readers for its fields but no automatically supplied writers.

before: A condition that must hold after a structural pattern matches.
after: An extra condition that must be true after the pattern matches.

before: Assigning components of a value to several local names, optionally gathering a remainder.
after: Give different parts of a collection separate local names.

before: Loading a trusted Ruby feature relative to the source file, with require’s once-per-feature behavior.
after: Load a file relative to the file containing the call. A previously required file is not loaded again.

before: Invoking a named public method using public_send; authorization still requires a separate policy.
after: Choose a method by name while allowing only a public method call.

before: An instance method installed with define_method whose block can capture lexical locals.
after: A method defined with a block can keep access to local values around that block.

before: A lexically scoped alteration to method lookup activated with using.
after: A changed version of behavior that applies in code where the refinement is active.

before: The region and exception classes a handler actually covers.
after: Handle a matching exception from the protected part of the code.

before: Restarting an exception-protected operation only under an explicit finite policy.
after: Try failed work again, with a rule that limits how often it can repeat.

before: Retaining original elements differs from replacing each element with a computed result.
after: Selection keeps some items. Transformation computes a result from each selected item.

before: The explicitly carried partial result updated once per element.
after: The running value carried from one step of a reduction to the next, such as a total.

before: Demand-driven computation limited before collecting results.
after: Ask a lazy sequence for only the number of items you need.

before: A parenthesized matching subexpression whose text is available in MatchData.
after: A part of a pattern in parentheses that remembers the text it matched.

before: Distinguishing encoded bytes from characters and validating their interpretation.
after: The encoding tells Ruby how bytes represent characters. A byte count and a character count can differ.

before: A resource whose lifetime ends automatically when its owning block exits.
after: A resource, such as a file, that the operation cleans up when its block finishes.

before: Removing a temporary file as well as closing its handle.
after: Close and remove a temporary file when the task that uses it ends.

before: Checking parsed container and field types and domain constraints after syntax succeeds.
after: Check that parsed data has the fields and types the task expects.

before: A field whose delimiter characters are protected by CSV quoting.
after: A CSV field in quotes can contain a comma without being split into two fields.

before: One time point can have different local clock fields without changing the instant.
after: One moment can be shown using different local dates and times.

before: Parsing a typed option does not establish that its value belongs to the allowed domain.
after: Turning an option into a number does not prove that number is within the allowed range.

before: A named executed assertion provides narrower evidence than merely starting a test command.
after: An assertion checks one expected answer. Its result is evidence about that check.

before: A version rule that filters candidates without proving behavioral compatibility.
after: A rule limiting which versions of a package a project accepts.

before: A shared-state operation guarded as one invariant-preserving region.
after: A section of code where a lock protects shared data from competing updates.

before: A synchronized handoff with finite buffering and an explicit completion protocol.
after: A queue that can hold only a set number of waiting items. A producer may wait until room opens.
